Psychology: rehabilitation and disability

Adaptation, participation, autonomy and environmental barriers.

What it does

Rehabilitation psychology supports people with physical, sensory, intellectual or psychosocial disabilities, and people who have had an injury or illness that changes their lives, such as a stroke, a head injury or a spinal cord injury. Its aim is not only to restore functions but to achieve the greatest possible autonomy, participation and quality of life.

Where it works

  • Hospitals and neurorehabilitation centres.
  • Day centres, early intervention and independent living support services.
  • Job placement and supported employment.
  • Associations of disabled people and their families.

What research has contributed

  • Disability also depends on the environment: the WHO's International Classification of Functioning (2001) describes how physical and social barriers limit participation as much as the impairment itself.
  • Cognitive rehabilitation: training attention, memory or executive functions, and using external aids such as diaries or alarms, improves daily life after brain injury.
  • Supported employment: seeking real work as early as possible, with a job coach, gives better results than long periods of prior training.
  • Positive behaviour support: understanding what a challenging behaviour is for and changing the environment reduces such behaviour in people with intellectual disabilities.

An example

Many people who acquire a disability describe a better adjustment than those around them expected. This is known as the "disability paradox": the quality of life they report is often higher than health professionals predict. This does not mean there are no difficulties, but that people find new ways of giving meaning to their lives, especially when they have support.

From the medical model to rights

The United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (2006), ratified by Spain in 2008, changed the approach: the aim is no longer to "fix" the person but to guarantee their rights and remove barriers. The movement's motto sums up this idea: "Nothing about us without us".

References

  1. Organización Mundial de la Salud (2001). Clasificación Internacional del Funcionamiento, de la Discapacidad y de la Salud (CIF). Ginebra: OMS.
  2. Albrecht, G. L. y Devlieger, P. J. (1999). The disability paradox: High quality of life against all odds. Social Science & Medicine, 48(8), 977–988.
  3. Cicerone, K. D. et al. (2019). Evidence-based cognitive rehabilitation: Systematic review of the literature from 2009 through 2014. Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, 100(8), 1515–1533.
  4. Bond, G. R., Drake, R. E. y Becker, D. R. (2008). An update on randomized controlled trials of evidence-based supported employment. Psychiatric Rehabilitation Journal, 31(4), 280–290.
